content:
A student died. A family is asking questions. A professor is facing serious allegations.

And somewhere between all three, the truth still has to be established.

The death of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode has stayed with me, not simply because I am a law student, but because I am a student first.

On September 18, Sahil, a second-year student, died by suicide hours after he was allegedly found using a mobile phone and ChatGPT during an examination. IIT Bombay has said no disciplinary action had been initiated against him.

His parents, however, have alleged something much deeper: that Sahil had been subjected to caste-based remarks and harassment before his death. IIT Bombay has denied the caste-discrimination allegation and said Sahil had not previously complained to its SC/ST cell or administration.

An FIR has since been registered against a professor for alleged abetment of suicide, with provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act also invoked. The investigation has been transferred to the Mumbai Crime Branch.

As someone studying criminal law, this is where I think we need to be very careful.

An FIR is not a conviction.

An allegation should not become a verdict merely because it is serious.

But equally, an allegation of caste-based harassment should not be dismissed before it has been properly investigated.

Due process has to work in both directions.

It must give a grieving family the space to have serious allegations investigated fairly.

And it must ensure that the person accused is not treated as guilty before evidence establishes responsibility.

But beyond the legal questions, I keep coming back to Sahil.

Before this became an FIR, a protest, an investigation or a debate about the SC/ST Act, there was a young student who was evidently going through something.

That raises another question for our educational institutions.

When a student faces an academic or disciplinary crisis, what happens in the hours immediately after?

Who speaks to them?

Who checks whether they are emotionally safe?

Who makes sure that one mistake, allegation or moment of panic does not feel like the end of everything?

Students are now demanding reforms including stronger grievance-redressal mechanisms and round-the-clock psychiatric support on campus.

Perhaps this case needs us to resist choosing a side before the investigation does its work.

Investigate the family's allegations seriously.

Protect the professor's right to due process.

Examine the institution's response.

And most importantly, ask whether there were moments when a young person needed help and the system failed to recognise them.

Justice here cannot simply mean deciding who was right and who was wrong.

It must also mean understanding what happened well enough to prevent another student, another family and another campus from reaching this point.

#LawStudent #DueProcess #SCSTAct #StudentWelfare #LegalEducation #CriminalLaw #Justice
comment: Institutions often focus on rules after a crisis, but the stronger test is whether early warning systems, confidential reporting, and student support mechanisms work before a crisis escalates.
